opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think worst-of-N is one of the more underappreciated ways to look at these results, and honestly it's the one I find most meaningful from a safety standpoint. The headline numbers people usually quote are average performance, how the model does on a typical attempt. But in health, the typical case isn't really what keeps you up at night. If you ask a model the same question several times and one of those responses tells someone it's fine to wait on symptoms that actually need urgent care, that's the response that matters. So worst-of-N asks: if you sample the model N times, how good is the worst answer you get? That's much closer to reliability than to capability.

What's encouraging is that we've seen real movement on that metric across model generations. The gap between average performance and worst-case performance has been narrowing. Newer models aren't just getting smarter on average; their bad tail is getting thinner. That's a different kind of progress, and arguably a more important one for deployment, because a lot of the harm in health comes from inconsistency rather than from a model that's uniformly mediocre.

That said, I'd be careful not to over-read it. Worst-of-N still drops off as you increase N, which tells you there's meaningful variance left in these systems. And the evaluation is only as good as the rubrics and scenarios behind it. If the scenarios don't capture the messy, underspecified way real people describe their health concerns, you can look robust on the benchmark and still have failure modes in the wild.

So my read is that it's a genuine signal that reliability is improving, not just raw knowledge, but also a reminder of how much headroom remains. If I had to pick one number to track for whether health AI is ready for higher-stakes use, I'd probably watch worst-case behavior over average-case scores, and I'd want to see it keep closing that gap.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it cuts against the way people usually talk about progress in this space. The headline number for a health AI model is almost always some kind of average: average accuracy on a benchmark, average physician preference rating, mean score on a rubric. And those averages have been going up steadily, which is genuinely exciting. But worst-of-N is asking a different question. If you sample the model N times on the same case, or you look across N different patients, how bad is the worst response you get? And in medicine, that's the question that actually matters, because a patient doesn't experience the average. They experience one interaction, and if that's the one where the model confidently misses a red flag, the average doesn't help them.

What we've seen is that the worst-of-N results tend to lag the average results, sometimes by a lot. You can have a model that looks excellent on mean performance and still, when you dig into the tail, find responses that a clinician would consider unacceptable. And interestingly, the gap doesn't always close just by scaling the model or improving the average. You can push the mean up and the tail stays stubborn, because the failures are often concentrated in rare presentations, ambiguous cases, situations where the model should express uncertainty or defer and instead fills the gap with something plausible-sounding.

So my interpretation is that worst-of-N is a more honest proxy for real-world safety than the numbers we usually report, and I think it should reframe how we define progress. Progress isn't just the mean going up. It's the tail coming up with it, and the variance shrinking. That has implications for how we train, so you're explicitly optimizing against those worst cases rather than letting them hide in the average. It has implications for evaluation, where you want to specifically construct the hard, atypical, high-stakes cases rather than sampling what's common. And it has implications for deployment, because if the tail hasn't caught up, you need the system design around the model to catch it, whether that's clinician oversight, abstention, or escalation paths.

The optimistic read is that we now have the tools to actually measure this, and once you can measure it you can improve it. The sobering read is that a lot of the apparent progress in the field has been measured in a way that systematically flatters the models. I'd rather we be clear-eyed about that, because the whole point is to make something that's trustworthy for the patient who draws the unlucky sample.

astra-6.text:
I think the worst-of-N results are a useful reminder that average performance isn’t the whole story, especially in health. A model can give a really impressive answer most of the time, but if you sample it repeatedly and some of those answers contain serious mistakes, that matters. You want to understand how bad those failures are and how often they happen.

The encouraging kind of progress would be seeing those worst answers improve alongside the average answer. That would suggest we’re making the model more reliable, rather than just more capable of producing a great response. But I’d be careful about treating worst-of-N as a direct measure of clinical risk. It depends on how many samples you take, what questions you ask, and how you judge the answers. It’s a useful stress test, and it needs to sit alongside evaluation in the actual setting where the model will be used.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the worst-of-N results are a useful reminder that progress in health AI isn’t just about how good the average answer is. It’s also about what happens when the model has a bad moment. If you sample several responses and look at the weakest one, you’re testing a different property: how reliably does the model stay within the bounds of acceptable behavior?

In health, that matters a lot. A model can give an excellent answer most of the time, but a rare, consequential mistake can still be a serious problem. So I’d interpret improvements on worst-of-N as evidence that we’re making progress on reliability, alongside capability.

But I wouldn’t equate that with proving clinical safety. You still need to understand what the failures are, how consequential they are, and whether the evaluation reflects the situations people actually encounter. The encouraging direction is models getting better at recognizing uncertainty, asking for missing information, and knowing when someone needs professional care.
